title: GroundTruth: what the ground knows about the week

beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Every one of you shook the ground on the way here. By car, by bus, on foot. A few billionths of a metre, but you did. And somewhere under this city, an instrument wrote it down. Here's one day of that writing.

beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: One whole day under Brussels, midnight to midnight. Look at the morning. Weekday, or weekend? (one beat, don't wait) It was a Wednesday: Christmas Day, 2019. Our model said Sunday. In a few minutes you'll see why it was right to be wrong.

beats.title: Last time: one question
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Two months ago we asked one question: can a seismometer tell what day it is? We made five promises. Short answer: we kept all five, then kept going. So, what is it actually hearing?
beats.screen: A still: last time's question and the five promises.

beats.title: What a seismometer records
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Every car, bus and footstep pushes on the ground and sends a tiny wave down through the rock. A seismometer is a weight on a spring: the ground moves, the weight lags, and it measures the difference. Seismologists built these for earthquakes, and everything else they call noise. This is an ordinary Wednesday in January 2020 under Brussels: quiet at night, a jump at seven, high all day. The noise is a city waking up. Shraddha, who else has listened?

beats.title: Who listened to cities before us
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: We're not the first to listen to cities. In 2017, a team in Barcelona traced city noise to traffic, the metro and crowds. (Next) Then the pandemic. In Tokyo, four years of recordings showed weekday daytime noise recovered quickly after the first state of emergency, and Sundays more slowly. (Next) And most recently, people map it street by street with fifty kilometres of fibre-optic cable, as in San Jose.
beats.screen: Row 1: Díaz 2017, Barcelona.
presses: Row 2: Nimiya 2021, Tokyo
Row 3: Liu 2025, San Jose

beats.title: Where they stopped, and where we start
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: docs/02-data-and-sources.md, "Papers" and "Where this project goes beyond the papers"
beats.notes: So where did they stop? They measured averages: an hour, a type of day, a lockdown. We guess one day at a time, graded only on weeks the model never saw. They studied one city or one event; we used 149 seismometers, then 33 cities over seven years, and tested a city the model never heard. (Next) They needed phone data to compare with; our model needs none, and its own mistakes find holidays without labels. They removed people to see earthquakes; we kept people as the signal, and tested that idea on earthquakes too. It didn't help, and we'll show you. (Next) And they needed dense arrays or new fibre; we use seismometers that are already in the ground, and a test runs every night. Aradhya, where do ours come from?
beats.screen: Rows 1–2: averages vs one day at a time; one city vs 149 seismometers and 33 cities.
presses: Rows 3–4: phone data vs no phones; removing people vs keeping them
Row 5: dense arrays or fibre vs seismometers already in place

beats.title: Seismometers on six continents
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Here they are: 158 seismometers on six continents, one reading every fifteen minutes, late 2019 to mid-2020. (touch Brussels) Brussels is this one, in Uccle. Holidays and lockdown are set aside, which leaves 17,027 ordinary days to learn from. So whose recordings are these?
beats.screen: The live research map, 158 dots (if it hasn't loaded in 5 s, the globe clip plays instead). Touch Brussels with one finger: its card shows the network and its DOI.

beats.title: Where every recording comes from
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Every recording has an owner. The 2019 to 2020 recordings are Lecocq and colleagues' published data. (Next) Everything since, 2019 to today, comes from EarthScope's public noise spectra; the earthquakes from the US Geological Survey's catalogue; and holidays and weekends from public calendars, never from the shaking itself. (Next) Behind them are 59 seismic networks, and 54 have a DOI you can cite. On the website, click any station and it shows its network and DOI.
beats.screen: Box 1: Lecocq et al. (2020) → used for the 2019–20 models.
presses: Boxes 2–4: EarthScope MUSTANG, USGS ComCat, public calendars
The 59 network codes; dashed ones have no DOI

beats.title: Two kinds of shaking
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Not all shaking is us. The slow wobbles, one every few seconds, are the ocean, waves hitting coasts hundreds of kilometres away. The fast ones, several a second, are engines, wheels and feet.

beats.screen: The clip plays by itself: “Two kinds of shaking”, the coast. It stops on “Slow: ocean waves…” with big blue rings.
presses: Stops on “Fast: engines, wheels and feet” with small orange rings from the cars

beats.title: The sea keeps no office hours
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: R12 data, Brussels (BE.UCC), Oct 2025 – Sep 2026, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: Held still. Left, the ocean: 11 a.m. and 3 a.m. are almost the same line; the sea doesn't keep office hours. Right, 4 to 14 hertz: daytime is about forty times stronger than night. That gap is us, so that's the band we listen to.
beats.screen: A still: the spectrum, the sea band against the people band.

beats.title: The sea band can't read the week
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: And we tested it. Same model, same days, five bands. The ocean band reads weekday vs weekend 51% of the time: a coin toss. Every band where people are scores above 95%, and the people band, 4 to 14 hertz, is best: almost 99%. Shraddha, how does a model listen?
beats.screen: A still: five bands; the sea band is a coin toss, the people band almost 99%.

beats.title: From the ground to a guess
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: Before the details, the whole method on one page: the six steps of our methodology document. (step 1) The data: each day becomes one row, only the 4 to 14 hertz band, glitches dropped, every clock moved to local time. Then 25 features. Then the labels: weekends and holidays come from public calendars, and only ordinary days ever train. (Next) The model: a forest of a hundred trees votes on the day, and we only grade it on whole weeks it never saw. (Next) And step six turns its surprise into a detector of unusual days. The next slides open these steps one by one.
beats.screen: Row 1: Steps 1–3 (one row per day, 25 features, calendar labels).
presses: Steps 4–5: random forest, honest testing
Step 6: unusual days

beats.title: One day becomes 25 numbers
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: The first boxes, up close. A model can't look at a picture, so each day becomes 25 numbers. Twenty-four say when the city was busy, hour by hour: the shape. One says how loud the whole day was compared with that station's usual day: the level. Every station is different, some by a motorway, some in a basement; the shape is what makes them comparable.

Stops on “4. Split the day: shape and level”
Ends on “24 + 1 = 25 numbers per day”

beats.title: A hundred trees vote
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: The next box: the model is a random forest, a hundred decision trees, each asking a few yes/no questions. A real one from Brussels: at six in the morning, was the ground still no busier than the rest of the day? Yes leads to weekend. On a Wednesday it never saw, 97 of 100 trees say weekday, but they split on which weekday.

The trees vote: the tally fills in, “97 of 100 say weekday”
Ends on “But only 5 say Wednesday…”

beats.title: Graded only on weeks it never saw
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: And the last box: grading. We never grade it on a week it studied. Monday and Tuesday are near-twins, so we hide whole weeks, five rounds. And we score it so that always guessing weekday gets 50, not five out of seven: balanced accuracy. Aadit, how did it do?
beats.screen: A still: the calendar of weeks, each shade one round's hidden weeks.

beats.title: How one guess is made
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: Brussels (BE.UCC), Wednesday 15 January 2020; forest trained only on other weeks (forest.json)
beats.notes: So how does one guess actually happen? Take a day the model has never seen: Wednesday the 15th of January 2020, in Brussels. Its 25 numbers go in: 24 for the shape of the day, one for its level. (Next) Each of the hundred trees asks its own few yes/no questions and casts one vote. These are the real votes: 31 Friday, 25 Tuesday, 23 Monday, only 5 Wednesday, and 3 for the weekend. (Next) So the exact-day guess is Friday: wrong. But 97 of 100 trees agree it's a weekday: right. That's this model in one day: sure about the weekend, unsure which weekday. Aadit, what does it look at?
beats.screen: The day's 25 numbers → 100 trees.
presses: The real votes appear: Mon 23, Tue 25, Wed 5, Thu 13, Fri 31, Sat 3, Sun 0
The two answers: “Which day? Friday. Wrong” and “Weekday or weekend? Weekday. Right”

beats.title: What the model looks at
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Brussels, all 115 ordinary days; scikit-learn feature_importances_ (impurity decrease); ml.json
beats.notes: Which of the 25 numbers does the forest lean on? This is Brussels. Each bar is how much that number helps the trees split the days. (Next) The tallest: midnight, one in the afternoon, and six in the morning. Our reading: six a.m. asks whether the city has woken up yet. And the level, how loud the whole day was, ranks only tenth. The shape of the day is what carries the week.
beats.screen: 25 grey bars: how much each number helps.
presses: The top three hours turn black (00:00, 06:00, 13:00), and the line “the level ranks 10 of 25”

beats.title: Where it gets it wrong
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Out-of-fold guesses: Brussels, GroupKFold by week (ml.json); all seismometers, outputs/tables/day_scores.csv
beats.notes: So where does it go wrong? This is a confusion matrix: each row is the real day, each column the model's guess, and the diagonal is right. Brussels, 115 ordinary days, each guessed by a model that never saw its week. (Next) Two blocks. Weekdays blur into each other: a Tuesday is often called a Monday. But the weekend stands apart: right 28 times out of 32, and a weekday is called a weekend only once in 83 days. (Next) And it's not just Brussels: across all 149 seismometers, 16,554 days, the same two blocks. That's why weekday-or-weekend is our headline, and the exact day is the hard part.
beats.screen: Brussels' 7×7 confusion matrix, in counts.
presses: The two blocks are outlined (weekdays orange, weekend blue) with three lines underneath
The second matrix: all 149 seismometers, in %

beats.title: It reads the day
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: One forest per seismometer. Weekday or weekend: 95% in a typical city. The exact day: 47%, where guessing gets 14. In three of the emptiest places in the data, a mountain, the Kalahari, the tip of Chile, it's near chance. No people, no rhythm. And the shape matters: loudness alone names the exact day 30% of the time; with the shape, 47%.
beats.screen: A still: 95% weekday or weekend, 47% exact day; every seismometer as a dot.

beats.title: Its mistakes find holidays
beats.speaker: Aradhya, Aadit
beats.notes: [Aradhya] Back to Christmas: a Wednesday it had never seen, and it said Sunday, and so did the models at 71% of seismometers. On weekday holidays it never saw, it said weekend 76% of the time; on ordinary weekdays, 5%. It learned how people behave, not the calendar. [Aadit] Rank every day by how surprised it was, and the holidays float to the top. Here is how that works.

Stops on “Confusion = 1 − P(the real day). Brussels' most surprising days”

beats.title: From a mistake to an alarm
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Results 7 and 8; groundtruth/detect.py (95th percentile of out-of-fold ordinary days)
beats.notes: How does a mistake become an alarm? Follow Christmas through the boxes. A day it never saw: a Wednesday. The forest says Sunday, and gives Wednesday no chance at all. (Next) So how surprised is it? One minus the chance it gave the real day: one, the maximum. (Next) Then compare that with ordinary days: ninety-five out of a hundred are less surprising than this line. Above the line, flag it. No labels, no list of holidays. Across every seismometer, that alarm beat the standard unusual-day alarm at 110 of 147. We never built a holiday detector. We taught it normal.
beats.screen: Boxes 1–2: a new day (Christmas 2019) → the forest guesses Sunday.
presses: Box 3: surprise = 1.00
Boxes 4–5: above 95% of ordinary days → flag it; then 76% and 110 of 147

beats.title: It recognises rest, not the name of the day
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: A model trained on all the other cities still reads a new one: 83%. Trained only on Saturday-Sunday countries, it calls Salfit's Fridays weekend: it recognises rest, not the name of the day. Jeddah, our third Friday city, didn't transfer. And when the UAE moved its weekend in 2022, we wrote the prediction down before downloading anything: Sundays got 20% quieter, luck would do that about 3 times in 1,000. One sensor, 90 km from Sharjah city, and Fridays got 53% busier, which we didn't predict.
beats.screen: A still: the weekend moves (Salfit and the UAE).

beats.title: The dare, done properly
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: Result 19 (docs/17) and the second-by-second test (docs/20), both written down before running
beats.notes: Last time's dare: if we know what a city sounds like at eight on a Tuesday, can we subtract the people and find small earthquakes underneath? On fifteen-minute averages: not supported, p = 0.053, and outside one Puerto Rico swarm a simple rolling median did best. A quake lasts seconds; fifteen minutes blurs it away. So we wrote a proper test down in advance: second-by-second recordings, years the first test never touched, at most 100 quakes per station so no swarm decides it. Result: with the people subtracted, 413 found; the raw recording, 501. Not supported: it made things worse. A plain rolling baseline of the last five minutes did best, 524. A city's weekly rhythm is the right model for reading the day, and the wrong one for finding a quake that lasts seconds. Detecting quakes that happened; never predicting them. Shraddha, what else didn't work?

beats.title: What didn't work
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: Three honest ones. Lockdown didn't make weekdays look like Sundays: only about a quarter were called weekend; it looked like no day the model had heard. Our shape-plus-level split doesn't beat raw hourly numbers; it's about as good, and easier to compare. And all of this is one season, with national holidays only. So: what happens with years?
beats.screen: A still: three things that didn't work.

beats.title: Now scale it
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Results 15–17, Jan 2019 – Sep 2026, 33 cities, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: We went back to the source: seven years, every station from the study that is still recording and publicly served, plus Sharjah. 33 cities, 72,000 ordinary days. This is a new, bigger model: three frequency bands, every half hour, gradient boosting, still tested only on weeks it never saw. A new experiment, so new numbers.
beats.screen: A still: 33 cities, 7 years, the ordinary days.

beats.title: More data helps, then flattens
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: Results 16–18, 2019–26, 33 cities, every score on weeks the model never saw
beats.notes: The obvious bet: seven years makes it much smarter. Weekend or not: 97%. But the exact day climbs from 38% at 100 days to 57% with all of them, and flattens. One model for all 33 cities together: worse in every city. A Tuesday just sounds like a Thursday. Show it the week around the day instead: 96%.
beats.screen: A still: the learning curve from 100 days to all of them, and 96% for the week.

beats.title: Everything we built
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Everything you've seen runs on one website, built from these same files. Two sources of data, one set of Python code, and a GitHub Action every morning. (Next) And the pages that keep going: City Pulse, which scores yesterday every night; a game where you try to beat the model; and pages that explain how it works and where it stops. The front page first.

beats.title: Ask the ground
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Here it is, live: 33 cities, any day from 2019 to last September. (Brussels, Christmas 2019) From the day alone: Sunday, sure of it. From the week around it: Wednesday, sure of it. beats.title: What runs every night
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: So how does a website know what the ground did last night? Follow the boxes. The seismometers record all day; EarthScope publishes their spectra about two days later; and every morning at six, a GitHub Action wakes up and downloads the new days. (Next) Two models score each day: the frozen one, trained on one year and never changed, and a learner that guesses a day first and only then studies it. (Next) The answers are saved in the repository, Vercel publishes them, and the globe, Ask and City Pulse read them. Ask's seven-year models are built once on a laptop and saved the same way. Here it is running.
beats.screen: Seismometers → EarthScope → GitHub Action.

beats.title: Still useless?
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: So: seismometers. Still useless? There's a network already buried under many of the world's cities, recording for decades, free. It hears a neighbourhood, not a person: no phones, no cameras. And ours is running tonight. Everyone measures how loud the ground is. We taught a model what normal sounds like, and its mistakes tell us when something happened. That's GroundTruth. Thank you.
